proposal.comment: [Playbook] The Agreement has no indemnification section at all, although Sections 9.3 and 19.4 already assume one (including the Section 20.5 infringement remedies). We have inserted our standard Section 20: Vendor defends third-party IP, breach-of-law, data-breach and wilful-misconduct claims, with usual exclusions, a reciprocal but narrow Customer indemnity, and the procure/modify/replace/refund remedies the rest of the document cross-references.

ops.text: 20.1 Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services, Deliverables, or Vendor Technology infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to, use, or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor or its personnel, Affiliates, or subcontractors; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct.

20.2 Vendor's obligation under Section 20.1(a) does not apply to the extent a claim arises from Customer's modification of the Services or Deliverables other than as authorized by Vendor, combination of the Services or Deliverables with items not supplied or recommended by Vendor where the claim would not have arisen but for the combination, or Vendor's compliance with written specifications supplied by Customer.

20.3 Customer shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Vendor from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that content or materials provided by Customer to Vendor infringe or misappropriate a third party's intellectual property right, or (b) Customer's breach of Applicable Law. Customer has no other indemnification obligation under this Agreement.

20.4 The indemnified Party shall give the indemnifying Party prompt written notice of the claim (provided that delay relieves the indemnifying Party only to the extent it is materially prejudiced), permit the indemnifying Party to control the defence with counsel reasonably acceptable to the indemnified Party, and provide reasonable cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense. The indemnified Party may participate with its own counsel at its own cost. The indemnifying Party shall not settle a claim in a manner that imposes a non-indemnified obligation or liability on, or requires an admission by, the indemnified Party without its prior written consent.

20.5 If a claim described in Section 20.1(a) is made or is reasonably likely, Vendor shall, at its expense and at Customer's election, procure for Customer the right to continue using the affected item, or modify or replace it with a functionally equivalent, non-infringing item that continues to meet the requirements of this Agreement. If neither remedy is reasonably available within thirty days, Customer may terminate the affected Services, Deliverables, or Order Form and Vendor shall refund prepaid Fees for the terminated items and Fees paid for Deliverables Customer can no longer reasonably use.

proposal.summary: Insert missing Section 20 (Indemnification): Vendor IP/misconduct indemnity, standard exclusions and procedure, narrow Customer indemnity, and the Section 20.5 infringement remedies already cross-referenced.

quote: Customer may terminate an Order Form immediately if Vendor suffers a material Security Incident, repeatedly misses a critical service level, violates Applicable Law in performing the Services, or infringes a third party's intellectual property and cannot provide the remedies required by Section 20.5.
rationale: The Agreement contains no indemnification or hold-harmless clause anywhere: searches for "indemnif", "hold harmless", and "defend" return only incidental references (Section 19.4 carve-out for "indemnified claims", Section 21.3 treating "indemnification obligations" as Excluded Claims, and Section 30.5 preserving indemnified-party rights). Section 20 is entirely absent from the outline even though Sections 9.3 and 19.4 rely on it, and Section 9.3 expressly cross-references "the remedies required by Section 20.5", leaving a broken reference. With no Vendor IP indemnity at all, the document sits in walk-away territory under this rule. We therefore propose inserting a Section 20 at the preferred position: Vendor defence/indemnity for third-party IP, breach of law, Vendor-caused data breach and gross negligence/wilful misconduct; customary exclusions (Customer modifications, combinations, Customer specifications); standard notice/control/cooperation procedure; a narrow Customer indemnity limited to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law; and procure/modify/replace/refund remedies in Section 20.5 to restore the existing cross-reference.

Vendor keeps its pre-existing Vendor Technology under Section 14.3, and the perpetual licence in Section 13.2 continues to cover any Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable; if ownership is not workable, our fallback is Vendor ownership plus a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence for us to use, modify and sublicense Deliverables for our business.

quote: 14.2 Vendor exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer. Customer receives a revocable, non-transferable licence to use a Deliverable only during the applicable Order Form term.
rationale: Section 14.1 preserves our ownership of Customer Data and pre-existing IP, and Section 14.4 bars joint ownership, so those elements are fine. But Section 14.2 gives Vendor exclusive ownership of every Deliverable created specifically for us (as defined in Section 1.4) with only a revocable, non-transferable licence limited to the Order Form term. That fails both the preferred position (Customer owns deliverables, Vendor assigns) and the fallback (perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables). Section 13.2's perpetual licence does not cure it: by its terms it covers software and Vendor Technology delivered paid-up or embedded in a Deliverable, not the Deliverable itself, and Section 14.3 confirms that limited scope. Redline flips ownership to Customer with an express assignment while leaving Vendor Technology with Vendor under Sections 14.3 and 13.2.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: Section 21 meets the preferred position. The cap is expressly mutual and set at the greater of (a) Fees paid or payable by Customer in the twelve months preceding the event and (b) USD 1,000,000. Section 21.2 is a mutual exclusion of indirect/consequential damages, with helpful direct-damage carve-ins for data restoration, replacement services, notification and incident response. Section 21.3 defines "Excluded Claims" (which sit outside both the cap and the damages exclusion) to cover breach of confidentiality, data-protection or security obligations, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud, and infringement/misappropriation of the other Party's IP, and confirms Customer's obligation to pay undisputed Fees is not "damages" subject to the cap. "Fees" (§1.5) covers recurring subscription, professional services and usage fees, so the cap base is meaningful rather than illusory; §21.4 preserves independence and survival of each cap and exclusion, and §18.2 confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities. No competing or one-sided cap appears elsewhere in the document. No redline needed.

proposal.summary: Delete Section 7.2's disclose-and-match condition on engaging another provider (de facto exclusivity/ROFR).

quote: 7.2 Before engaging another provider, Customer must disclose and match for Vendor any more favourable commercial offer it receives.
rationale: Section 7.2 conditions our ability to engage any other provider on first disclosing and matching for Vendor any more favourable offer we receive. That is a de facto exclusivity / right-of-first-refusal binding the Customer: we cannot freely buy from another supplier without first routing the competing terms through Cobalt. It is unlimited in scope, applies for the full term, and has no performance-based exit, which is walk-away territory under this rule and fails the fallback (defined product category, 12 months, automatic end on service-level or delivery failure). It also directly contradicts Section 12.3, which states that Customer has made no exclusivity or most-favoured-customer commitment, so deletion of 7.2 restores internal consistency as well as the preferred position. The most-favoured-pricing aspect of the same sentence is addressed under the MFN rule and is not double-counted here; no other clause imposes exclusivity on us (Sections 13.1 and 14.2 concern licence scope and ownership, not supplier freedom).
